title: Read distributions and states over time

blocks.content: Explore four panels on Grafana Play to see the question each one answers.
Explore a histogram to see how its bars group values into numeric ranges, not named categories.

Focus on **Time series + Auto buckets**.

This panel answers the question: How many values fall in each range? Here the ranges are set automatically from the data. The horizontal axis is the value range, split into buckets. A bucket is one range of values, and each bar is one bucket. The vertical axis is the count of values in each bucket. Hover over a bar to read its bucket and count.

Compare a taller bar with a shorter one. The taller bar contains more values in its range. It doesn't necessarily contain the largest values. Position along the horizontal axis identifies the value range.

Its bars group numbers into ranges rather than named categories. It shows how many values fall in each range, but not when each value occurred.
Explore a heatmap to see how each cell combines a time, a span of numbers, and a count.

Find the **Linear** heatmap. This panel answers the question: How many values fall in each range, and how does that change over time?

Time runs along the horizontal axis. The size of the numbers runs up the vertical axis, and each row covers a span of numbers. Color shows how many values are in each cell, not whether something is healthy or unhealthy. A cell higher up covers bigger numbers, not more values.

Read the color legend rather than assuming darker or redder always means more, and hover over a cell to read its time, the span of numbers it covers, and its count.

Follow a band of colored cells from an earlier time to a later time. Notice whether the values stay in similar ranges or move higher or lower. The heatmap adds the timing that a single histogram leaves out.
Explore a state timeline to see how it joins matching states into one continuous bar.
Open the **State timeline and Status history** dashboard.

Find **State timeline strings**. This panel answers the question: What state has something been in, and when did it change?

Each row is one thing being tracked, such as **Level A**, and the horizontal axis is time. Follow **Level A** from left to right and read states such as LOW, HIGH, and NORMAL. Hover over a NORMAL bar to read its time span.

A bar's length represents duration rather than a numeric magnitude. This example merges consecutive equal values into one continuous bar. Read the state label. Color by itself doesn't define its meaning.

Explore a status history to see how it shows each value as its own box. State data is formatted as a table with timestamps, a name for what's being tracked, and a state value. The state can be a string, a number, or a boolean.

Focus on **Status history - boolean values**.

This panel answers the same question as the state timeline, one value at a time. Each row is a sensor, such as **SensorA**, and each box is one value at one moment in time. Hover over a box to read its boolean value and timestamp. What true and false mean depends on the sensor. True doesn't always mean healthy.

Adjacent boxes with the same value stay separate. Status history doesn't merge equal consecutive values into one bar the way a state timeline does.
